before.title: 6.4L HEMI Valvetrain Failure (Roller Lifter/Camshaft Wear, "HEMI Tick")
before.description: Gas RAM 2500s with the 6.4L (392) HEMI V8 suffer a documented valvetrain defect in which the roller lifter needle bearings fail, the roller stops rolling and drags across the camshaft lobe, wiping out the lobe. The failure is linked to the truck's Multi-Displacement System (MDS/cylinder deactivation): when cylinders are deactivated, oil delivery to the affected lifters is restricted, starving the roller bearings. Owners report onset as a metallic 'HEMI tick' progressing to misfire, dropped cylinder and catastrophic top-end damage. A class-action lawsuit (Petro, et al. v. FCA US LLC, Case No. 1:22-cv-00621, whose named plaintiffs include a 2020 RAM 2500 owner) alleges FCA knew of the defect since at least 2012 and failed to disclose it. There is no safety recall, so repairs typically fall on the owner once warranty lapses.
before.solution: Diagnosis via oil-analysis metal content, cylinder-specific misfire/lifter tick, and cam inspection. Accepted repair is replacement of all 16 lifters plus the camshaft (and any damaged pushrods/rockers); severely scored cams or circulated bearing debris often force a long-block or complete engine replacement. Many owners/shops disable/delete MDS during the rebuild to prevent recurrence. Frequent oil changes with correct-spec oil are the preventive measure.
symptoms: Metallic ticking/tapping from top of engine (HEMI tick)
Engine misfire, rough idle
Check engine light with misfire codes
Loss of power / dropped cylinder
Metal shavings in oil
Loud knocking as failure progresses

before.title: 6.7L Cummins EGR Cooler Clogging and Cracking
before.description: The EGR cooler routes hot exhaust through a coolant-jacketed heat exchanger before recirculating it into the intake. Heavy soot loading progressively plugs the cooler and EGR valve, first showing as slight off-idle hesitation and rising EGTs, then triggering EGR flow/performance codes and limp mode. Worse, a clogged, thermally stressed cooler can crack internally and leak coolant into the exhaust/intake stream, causing white smoke, coolant loss, and potential hydrolock or catastrophic engine damage. Cummins service intervals call for cleaning the EGR valve/cooler roughly every 67,500 miles (2007.5-2018) or 75,000 miles (2019+), which many owners never perform.
before.solution: Clean or replace the EGR cooler and valve. Genuine replacement cooler OEM PNs include 68048988AA (and related 4988885 / 4988884 / 68048991AA / 68444764AA for later trucks); an upgraded H-core cooler (e.g., BulletProof Diesel) resists cracking and clogging better than stock. Replace the EGR valve if the pintle is coked. Keep the DPF/regen system healthy, avoid excessive short-trip idling, and inspect/clean on Cummins' recommended interval to prevent the crack-and-coolant-loss failure mode.
symptoms: Hesitation off idle
Rising exhaust gas temperatures under load
White exhaust smoke / sweet coolant smell
Unexplained coolant loss
Check engine light with EGR flow codes
Reduced power / limp mode

before.title: 6.7L Cummins Grid Heater Bolt Failure (Bolt Drops Into Cylinder #6)
before.description: The intake grid (air) heater warms incoming air for cold starts and carries up to ~200 amps through a small threaded stud/bolt secured by a 10mm nut on the intake plenum. Over years of high-current heat cycling the bolt/nut connection deteriorates, arcs, and can break loose. Because it sits directly above the intake runner, gravity pulls the heavy steel stud straight into cylinder #6, destroying the piston, valves, and cylinder head, often the entire engine. Banks Power has documented 200+ failures, some at as little as 40,000 miles. Stellantis has NOT recalled the grid heater assembly itself (a separate 2021-2022 relay recall Y08/Y76 addressed sticking relays, not the bolt).
before.solution: Do the preventive 'wiggle test': with the engine off, grab the external power terminal (10mm bolt) and try to move it; any movement means the internal stud is loosening and needs immediate attention. Best fix is to replace the stock grid heater with a redesigned unit that eliminates the internal bolt, such as the BD Diesel Killer Grid Heater upgrade kit (PN 1041520, fits 2007-2024), or install a grid-heater delete/relocation plate (Fleece/Pusher) if legal in your area. Genuine Cummins intake air heaters (e.g., 3970000 / 3970001) are direct replacements but retain the original design.
symptoms: Loud engine knock / metallic clatter
Sudden power loss
Rough running or misfire on cylinder 6
Loose grid heater power terminal
Check engine light with grid heater codes
Hard cold starts

before.title: 6.7L Cummins VGT Turbo Actuator Failure
before.description: The Holset HE351VE variable-geometry turbocharger uses an electronically controlled actuator (the geartrain and control board that moves the vane sliding ring) that is a well-documented failure point, often before 100k miles. Soot and carbon buildup, rust/corrosion binding the vane arm, worn actuator gears, or a corroded circuit board (from coolant/water intrusion) cause the actuator to stop positioning the vanes correctly. The truck then either spools quickly but chokes at mid/high rpm or spools slowly with a big loss of low-end torque, and typically drops into limp mode. Owners on Cummins forums report repeat failures and note the unit must be scan-tool programmed to the specific turbo after replacement.
before.solution: Replace the VGT actuator with a genuine remanufactured Holset unit (common OEM/service PNs for 2007.5-2012: 2837675 / 4034315HX / 4046534 / 4049828; later 2013-2018 trucks use the updated HE300VG actuator). The new actuator MUST be calibrated/aligned and programmed to the turbo with a Cummins-capable scan tool (wiTECH) or a pre-programmed 'corded' plug-and-play unit such as the BD Diesel corded HE351 actuator. If the vane mechanism itself is seized with soot the whole turbo may need replacement. Clean the vanes/EGR side and address coolant leaks that corrode the board to prevent recurrence.
symptoms: Loss of power / limp mode
Slow or no turbo spool
Excessive turbo whistle or lack of boost
Check engine light with turbo actuator codes
Sluggish acceleration when towing
Actuator gear grinding/clicking on startup

before.title: 68RFE Torque Converter Shudder and TCC Failure
before.description: The 68RFE 6-speed automatic behind the Cummins is prone to torque converter shudder and lockup failure. The factory converter's clutch material and heat control are marginal for the Cummins' torque, so the torque converter clutch (TCC) chatters, slips, or refuses to hold lockup, felt as a low-speed vibration like driving over rumble strips. The TCC regulator valve wears its bore in the valve body, making apply pressure erratic. The resulting heat contaminates the fluid and cascades into planetary and clutch-pack damage. Heat is the number-one killer, especially when towing; fluid temps regularly over 200°F accelerate failure.
before.solution: Replace the torque converter with a stronger billet/multi-disc unit (e.g., Sun Coast, BD Diesel, or Suncoast triple-disc) rather than another stock converter. Rebuild or upgrade the valve body / TCC regulator valve (Sonnax) to restore correct apply pressure. Add an auxiliary transmission cooler and use the correct ATF+4 fluid, and consider a deep pan and improved fluid capacity for towing. Address early to avoid a full transmission rebuild.
symptoms: Shudder/vibration around 40-55 mph (converter lockup)

before.title: Center High-Mount Stop Lamp (Third Brake Light) Water Leak Into Cab
before.description: The center high-mounted third brake light on RAM 2500 trucks is a chronic water-leak point across both the 4th (2010-2018) and 5th (2019+) generations. before.title: 6.7L Cummins CP4.2 High-Pressure Fuel Pump Catastrophic Failure
before.description: The 2019+ RAM 2500 with the 6.7L Cummins diesel uses a Bosch CP4.2 high-pressure fuel injection pump that is prone to catastrophic self-destruction. The CP4.2 relies on diesel fuel for internal lubrication, and any contamination, water intrusion, or low fuel levels cause the pump to disintegrate, sending metal shavings throughout the entire fuel system. This contaminates fuel injectors ($500+ each x6), fuel rails, fuel lines, and the fuel tank, requiring a complete fuel system replacement costing $8,000-12,000+. Total cost: $8,000-12,000+ at dealer. Prevention: Install a FASS or AirDog lift pump system ($800-1,200) that provides additional fuel filtration and water separation before the CP4.2. Some owners proactively replace the CP4.2 with a CP3 conversion kit ($3,000-4,500) from S&S Diesel Motorsport or Fleece Performance for permanent reliability.

before.title: Diesel Exhaust Fluid (DEF) System Failures
before.description: The 2013+ RAM 2500 6.7L Cummins diesel DEF (Diesel Exhaust Fluid) system is plagued with failures of the DEF heater, DEF pump, DEF injector, NOx sensors, and SCR catalyst. If SCR catalyst is failed, replacement costs $2,000-3,500. Check TSB 18-018-20 for updated DEF heater and quality sensor procedures. Use only API-certified DEF fluid (ISO 22241 standard). Avoid storing DEF over 1 year as it degrades.

before.title: Front Axle Pinion Seal Leak (AAM Front Differential)
before.description: The American Axle (AAM) front differential on Ram 2500/3500 4x4 trucks is well known for recurring front pinion seal leaks. The pinion seal rides on a sleeve/wear surface on the pinion flange; over time the seal wears a groove into the sleeve, so simply installing a new seal on a grooved sleeve leaks again quickly. Owners on Cummins/Ram forums report going through multiple pinion seals. The same trucks also commonly leak at the axle-tube input/output shaft seals. Left unaddressed, gear oil coats the front driveshaft/underbody and the differential can run low on lubricant.
before.solution: Replace the front pinion seal AND the pinion flange sleeve (wear sleeve) together, not the seal alone, since a grooved sleeve will re-leak. Set pinion preload correctly on reassembly. Inspect the axle-tube/input shaft seals at the same time and replace if seeping. Use the correct gear oil and confirm the axle vent is not clogged (a plugged vent builds pressure and pushes oil past seals).

before.description: Ram 2500/3500 4x4 trucks with the American Axle (AAM) 9.25 front axle are known for premature front ball joint wear, sometimes as early as 25,000 miles. before.title: Front End "Death Wobble" Steering Oscillation
before.description: The RAM 2500 (and 3500) with solid front axle experiences a violent front-end oscillation known as "death wobble" that occurs at highway speeds (45-65 mph), typically triggered by hitting a bump or pothole. The steering wheel shakes uncontrollably and the entire front end vibrates violently, making the truck nearly undrivable until the driver slows to a stop. The issue is caused by worn or loose front-end components working together in resonance: track bar, ball joints, tie rod ends, unit bearings, steering stabilizer, and steering gear box. before.solution: Death wobble is a SYSTEM issue - all front-end components must be inspected. Start with: 1) Track bar and track bar bracket (most common initiator) - replace with upgraded aftermarket (Synergy, Carli) $200-400. 2) Ball joints - replace with Dynatrac or Synergy heavy-duty units $300-600/pair. 3) Tie rod ends - Moog or Synergy $100-200/pair. 4) Unit bearings - Timken or Moog $200-400/pair. 5) Steering stabilizer - Fox or Bilstein dual stabilizer $200-400. 6) Steering gear box - check for play, tighten or replace $400-1,200. Address ALL worn components, not just one. TSB 19-001-14 REV.B covers the inspection procedure.

before.title: HVAC Blend Door Actuator Failure (Clicking Dash, Uneven Cabin Temperature)
before.description: The HVAC blend-door actuators behind the RAM 2500 dash use small plastic gears that strip over time. When the gear teeth fail, the actuator motor repeatedly tries and fails to move the blend door, producing a persistent clicking/knocking noise from behind the dash and loss of temperature control — commonly one side of the cab blows hot while the other blows cold, or the system won't switch between heat and AC. If a new actuator still misbehaves, the HVAC control head/module is replaced instead. Note aftermarket actuators are weaker than OEM and may fail early.

before.title: Steering Gear Box Leak and Excessive Play
before.description: The RAM 2500/3500 steering gear box (power steering box) develops fluid leaks from the input shaft seal and sector shaft seal, and excessive play in the steering. The leak starts as a slow drip and worsens over time, eventually causing low power steering fluid and potential pump damage. Excessive play manifests as a "dead zone" in the steering where the wheel moves 1-2 inches without the wheels turning. The gear box also loosens from the frame due to the high stresses of the solid front axle design. Tightening the adjustment screw on the gear box can temporarily reduce play, but eventual replacement is needed.
before.solution: For minor leaks: Try a power steering stop-leak additive as a temporary fix ($15-20). For the input shaft seal leak, the seal can be replaced without removing the gear box ($100-200 labor). For excessive play: Adjust the sector shaft screw (1/4 turn clockwise) per TSB procedure - this takes up slack but is a temporary fix. For complete resolution, replace the steering gear box with OEM Mopar (68164717AA) or upgraded RedHead Steering Gear ($800-1,500 installed). Retorque or replace frame mounting bolts (they stretch over time).

before.title: TIPM (Totally Integrated Power Module) Failure
before.description: The TIPM is the central under-hood fuse/relay and power-distribution computer that controls the fuel pump, lighting, wipers, door locks, horn, and trailer-tow circuits. It is a widespread failure point on 2007-2016 Ram trucks. The most common complaint is the internal fuel pump relay sticking: stuck ON causes overnight battery drain and the pump running with the key off, while stuck OFF causes intermittent no-start / stalling. Other failures include inoperative wipers, dead door locks, non-working turn signals/high beams, phantom horn, and dead trailer lights. Root causes include water intrusion into the layered module and improperly spliced aftermarket accessories overloading circuits.
before.solution: Diagnose which circuit is affected before replacing. A stuck fuel pump relay can be temporarily addressed with an external fuel-pump relay bypass harness, but the durable fix is to rebuild the existing TIPM (specialist shops like Circuit Board Medics repair the boards/relays) or replace it with a new module that must be programmed to the VIN. Remove any improper accessory splices feeding off TIPM circuits. Inspect for and seal water intrusion at the module.

before.description: RAM 2500s fitted with the Uconnect 8.4-inch (RA3/RA4) head unit commonly suffer software and hardware faults: the touchscreen freezes or lags, the radio spontaneously reboots (audio cuts out and the Ram logo reappears), and some units fall into a continuous boot loop restarting every ~10 seconds (owners tie reboot loops to SiriusXM Travel Link and failed software updates). Separately, 'ghost touch' — the capacitive screen registering phantom inputs — is a hardware failure of the optically-clear adhesive (LOCA) between the digitizer and LCD that heat/sun break down, and no software reset fixes it. The problems span multiple model years and are a well-known chronic complaint.
before.solution: For freezes/reboots, first-line fix is a soft/hard reset (press-and-hold the volume/tuner knobs ~10-20 seconds) and installing the latest Uconnect software update. Persistent ghost-touch is hardware: replace the touchscreen digitizer (glass only, ~$50-150, no dealer programming) or the full head unit; a Mopar reman full unit must be VIN-programmed and dealer swaps run ~$1,500-2,000.
